title: Research field map
purpose: Map a research field so it can be looked at: what the field is made of, who works on it, and where the applied work is.

tool_notes.openalex: works, authors, institutions and concepts in one place, free and without a key — it carries most of the skeleton
tool_notes.crossref: publisher metadata, DOIs and funders, for what OpenAlex has not indexed
tool_notes.arxiv: preprints, which appear here months before anywhere else
tool_notes.a web-search tool: the only way to evidence a company — no free API lists what a private company is working on

kinds.meaning: a work — a paper, a preprint, a trial report. The thing a DOI identifies. Carries doi, and link when it has one
kinds.keywords: paper, article, preprint, study, work, DOI

kinds.meaning: a person who does the work
a subject, question or mechanism the field is about
a working group, usually inside an institution
a university, hospital or public body
a company, and what it is building

kind_notes.one word per thing: `publication` covers papers, preprints and trial reports — a kind is what a node IS, and the everyday words are keywords, not kinds. A graph may still split them (kind `preprint`) if it needs to; every kind renders, and a kind this app has never heard of gets its own colour.
kind_notes.older names: graphs built before this vocabulary may say `scientist` and `concept`; they render exactly the same way, with hash-derived colours. Nothing has to be migrated.

edges.label: authored
edges.meaning: the main link of a research field. --time the year

edges.label: targets
edges.meaning: what a company's work addresses, --dir in

edges.label: cites
edges.meaning: the citation skeleton: --from the citing work, --to the cited one, --dir in

edges.label: co-cited in N works
edges.meaning: two works cited together. Weak by nature: --power 0.05 --set cocited=N, so the count is data and the relation is drawn thin

edges.label: collaborates on <subject>
edges.meaning: two organisations on the same subject — this makes a cluster legible instead of a fan of lines into one dot

alternative.a work as an edge: a graph that prefers it may keep putting the work in the edge label (researcher → subject, label = the title, --time the year) instead of promoting it to a `publication` node. Both render; the node form carries a doi and can be co-cited, which the edge form cannot.

visuals.node weight: `weight` on a node is what it is worth on this map, and how it was measured is stated once for the whole graph in `meta.weight.metric` — "relevant papers", "thousands of citations (OpenAlex)". Every panel says which of the two a node's number came from: the document, or the graph's own connections. Change the metric and the sizes change; nothing else has to.
visuals.node size: with no `weight` and no `size`, a node is drawn from ½ × the summed power of its edges × a multiplier for its kind — publication 0.1, researcher 1, lab/institution/company 3, subject 10 — so a map is readable before anyone tunes it. Both halves are the graph's to change: `meta.weight.kind_multipliers`, or `weigh --mul subject=20`. `--set size=6` sets a node's weight by hand in the same units.
visuals.edge power: `power` is an edge's strength, where **1 is a normal relation**: `--set power=0.05` on a co-citation says it is texture, not structure, and it is drawn as a hairline at half opacity. A measured number is a different thing — `--set cocited=66` shows 66 in the panel and leaves the line as thin as it should be.
visuals.direction: `dir: in` puts an arrowhead at the `to` end, so a citation or a target reads as pointing at what it acts on.
visuals.level: a node's position on the third axis (foundational low, abstract high). The 3D view is the only place it moves anything; a 2D map laid out by rings or by force ignores it.
visuals.placement: `ring` puts a node on a concentric ring — 0 is the centre, higher numbers are further out — and `x`,`y` put it exactly where it is told. A graph with a ring on any node is laid out as rings; a graph where every node has `x`,`y` is used as given; otherwise the viewer lays it out itself.
visuals.default rings: organisations 0, researchers 1, publications 2, subjects 3 — which is the ask 'companies in the centre, researchers in the middle, subjects on the periphery' expressed as data.
visuals.following a graph: the panel lists a node's connections with the power and properties of each relation, strongest first. Clicking one opens that node and puts it in the middle of the view, so a graph can be walked rather than only looked at.

layout.note: Companies and institutions at the centre, researchers in the middle, subjects on the periphery. With authored x,y the viewer uses them as given; with `ring` it builds the rings; with neither it lays the graph out itself.
